To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
elderly patients with unbalance show a marked somatosensorial deficit, with a consequent impairment of the postural adaptation to destabilizing stimuli.
elderly people with balance disorders, in the majority of cases, present somatosensory impairment and a dysfunction of the flexor muscles.
the elderly people have a higher risk of falling due to somatosensorial and vestibular impairments, which can be improved by specific exercises and rehabilitation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dynamic postural control, and the postural adaptation to destabilizing perturbations in elderly subjects.
the study of dynamic stabilometric findings in the elderly with equilibrium disorders, and the results obtained are useful to better understand the postural strategies of this group of patients.
the evaluation of the functional integrity of the postural system in elderly people with balance disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in elderly people with unbalance, a more correct performance of postural responses is observed in the extensor muscles, which are less impaired by age-related degeneration.

in the elderly population with equilibrium disorders, the postural control is more impaired by the somatosensori-vestibular than by the visual subsystem, the postural strategy is more flexor than extensor and the postural adaptation to destabilizing stimuli is more impaired during support raising than lowering.

the elderly subject, in the presence of a balance disorder, should be considered as a subject with a "multisensor impairment" and with a "flexor muscle dysfunction", which is more evident in the lower limbs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the elderly subjects, in order to maintain their balance, have to rely more on visual than on vestibular information.
, in elderly subjects, the most frequent sensorial impairment is the somatosensorical one.
in elderly people, postural control is more impaired during lowering than during raising the support.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the somatosensorially impaired elderly patient, who is more prone to falling, is more likely to adopt a "flexor" strategy, rather than a "postural" strategy, to counteract destabilizing perturbations.
the somatosensorially mediated equilibrium control system is more impaired in elderly subjects with balance disorders than the vestibulocochlear system.
the elderly are more sensitive to destabilizing inputs.
